ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Easel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the easel through its card activity — setting up the artwork — so the child learns the full artist routine: prepare, paint, step back, look.

What is this?

An easel is a stand that holds paper upright while the artist works: clips on top, paint pots or a ledge below, and three or four legs to keep it steady. It is furniture for making things.

What does it mean?

Setting up teaches the routine before the art: paper first, then tools, then work. Standing to paint also changes the body — big shoulder movements replace small wrist ones.

What does the child need to know?

An easel (or a clipboard propped on a chair), paper, clips, and paint or markers. The setup is the lesson: let the child do every step.

Why this matters

The step-back-and-look habit is the most professional thing an artist does, and children learn it naturally at an easel — the work is at arm’s length, so viewing it means moving. That tiny habit is real self-evaluation, learned at two.

What it teaches

Sequencing (setup before art), big-motor strokes, independence — every step is child-sized — and the observing habit of stepping back to see the whole picture.

Words to learn

easelclipstanduprightstep backlookartiststudio

Say this to your child

“"This is our easel — real artists use these! Clip the paper... snap! Paint here, brush here. Now make big strokes — your whole arm is painting! Step back with me... LOOK at it. What does it need?"”

Step by step

  1. Bring the paper to the easel together and let the child work the clip — it is a finger workout.
  2. Set out the paints or markers below, one at a time, naming each choice.
  3. Stand beside the easel and paint or draw — whole arm, big strokes.
  4. Step back together two steps and look: what does the picture need now?
  5. Finish with the official artist move: one more look from far away, then sign it.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange easel stands on three legs with a blank canvas clipped at the top — the empty canvas is the invitation, and the ledge below is where the paint waits.

Ask your child

"What holds the paper tight?" (the clip) "Why do artists step back?" (to see the whole picture) "Show me a big easel stroke." "Where does the paint sit when we are not using it?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may announce "I’m working" and expect no interruptions, step back after every single stroke, or set up a stuffed animal beside the easel as a student — the studio now has staff.

Out in the real world

Every painter in every museum paints at an easel, and street portrait artists set theirs up in parks. The word easel comes from donkey — the patient animal that carries the load.

Try it together

Gallery hour: finish the easel painting, step all the way back, and walk the room past it like a visitor. Someone buys it — for a pretend number, paid in hugs.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes on first — paper or paint?" (paper) "Show me stepping back to look." "What does the clip do?" (holds the paper)

This lesson pairs with the Easel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
